claims.text: The onset and progression of the phase transition in solid FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles is governed by preferential copper segregation to the surface.
Surface-segregated copper forms a low-melting-point surface layer.
Melting initiates at the nanoparticle surface and subsequently propagates inward.
The as-synthesized FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are homogeneous solid solutions.
A thin inert surface coating can suppress copper segregation at the nanoparticle surface.
Untreated FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles form a copper-enriched surface layer during heating.
Copper's lower melting point, together with its surface segregation, locally reduces the melting point of the nanoparticle surface.
The locally reduced surface melting point induces surface premelting.
Surface premelting facilitates progression of melting from the outer shell to the nanoparticle core.
Nanoparticles treated to inhibit copper segregation will exhibit a later onset of surface premelting than untreated nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles treated to inhibit copper segregation will have a higher effective melting temperature than untreated nanoparticles.
Untreated nanoparticles will show early liquid formation at their surfaces because of copper segregation.
The proposed mechanism is relevant primarily when nanoparticle surface-to-volume effects dominate.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to bulk material or significantly larger particles.
Thermal history and initial homogenization may affect the magnitude of the proposed segregation-driven melting behavior.
